# Dimension values - GENERATED, DO NOT EDIT

Generated by `tools/dims.py md` from [`registry.toml`](registry.toml), which is
**authoritative for values**. Edit the registry, regenerate this.

The `machine/*.md` files stay authoritative for **reasoning** - why a number is what
it is, what it trades against, what was rejected. This table is only *what the numbers*
*are*. If a number in prose disagrees with this table, the prose is stale.

FLAG: IT DISAGREES WITH THE SUPPORT BLOCKS BY 8, AND ONE OF THE TWO IS WRONG. The Y screw axis can be reached two ways and they do not meet. Via the blocks: BF12 sits upside down with its base level with the interposer's underside, so the axis is Y_BEAM_UNDERSIDE - T_INTERPOSER - SCREW_AXIS_H = 182 - 10 - 25 = 147. Via the nut: the face is NUT_FACE_BELOW_BEAM under the beam and the axis NUT_AXIS_TO_FACE above it, so 182 - 63 + 20 = 139. Those are the two ends of ONE screw. The same 8 is in the as-built pair as well, which points at a constant being wrong rather than a slip. SCREW_AXIS_H's 25 is confirmed off the BF/BK12 spec - his, 2026-10-10 - so the error is on the nut side: either NUT_FACE_BELOW_BEAM is 8 too big or NUT_AXIS_TO_FACE is 8 too small. OPEN: NOTHING HERE HAS BEEN CHANGED TO MAKE IT CLOSE. THE MEASUREMENT THAT SETTLES IT: the nut housing's H, across the mounting face - if it is 40 then h is 20 and NUT_FACE_BELOW_BEAM moves to 55; if it is 56 then h is 28 and the nut chain was right all along. Measuring the built machine's beam underside down to the nut's mounting face does it just as well. WHAT IT WOULD ACTUALLY MOVE, and it is less than it looks. dims.py deps lists 14 dependents including all four BLOCK_*_COL, and reading that as “the sixteen bearing block holes move” is WRONG - his correction, 2026-10-10. RAIL_LOW_Z and RAIL_HIGH_Z are beam-local, measured off the beam’s bottom face; RAIL_LOW_XEP and the BLOCK_*_COL only re-express those same holes as coordinates from the PLATE’S BOTTOM EDGE. Move that edge and the numbers change while every hole stays exactly where it was against the beam. The only thing genuinely at stake is XEP_H - how far the X end plate runs down - and running 8 longer than it needs to is spare metal, not a fault. So this is worth getting right, but it is not a reason to hold up Sheet 2a. The half-of-H reasoning below is the part most likely to be the fault: it assumes the page’s H is 40 and that the bore is centred across it, and his 2026-10-10 figure for the nut across is 52, not 40. If H is really 56 this symbol is 28. SETTLED: THE CONVENTION IS THE SAME ONE BK-12 AND BF-12 USE for their h of 25, which is what lets these numbers be added up the way they are. It checks against the page’s own H of 40: the bore sits centred across that width, so h is half of it. This is the last term in the height chain at both ends of the machine - on Y the nut hangs and the face points down, on X the screw runs on top of the beam and the face points up. |

Even 0.3 across the nut's 40 mm bolt span is 0.43 degrees of tilt on a part that wants coplanarity in hundredths. Closed as SPACER_SKIM plus NUT_SHIM. FLAG: THE FOUR M5 CLEARANCE HOLES ALREADY GIVE THE NUT THE FLOAT IT NEEDS - 0.5 radial at Z_HOLE_D - so it self-centres on the screw as it is tightened. OPEN: IT IS ENOUGH ON ITS OWN wherever the bolt only has to cross a plate: on the Y sole bracket an M5 x 12 reaches 5.65 through the 1/4in bracket, and the aluminium thread is already stronger than the bolt at that depth. Tapping deeper is margin, not a fix - see NUT_TAP_DEPTH. |
| **NUT_TAP_REACH** | 14 mm | measured |  | 14, HOW FAR A BOLT ACTUALLY GOES into the tapped housing - and the measurement is the good part. FLAG: THAT MEASURES THE CONSEQUENCE, NOT THE ANNOUNCEMENT. The hole drills 16 but a plug tap cannot thread the last couple of millimetres of a blind hole, so the drilled depth was never the usable figure - and reasoning from it is exactly the error that put a wrong bolt in this file twice. One spare part and a bolt settled what two rounds of arithmetic did not. OPEN: IT IS THE TAP'S LIMIT, NOT THE HOLE'S - his, 2026-10-08: that was a plug tap, not a bottoming tap. So another millimetre or two is available if anything ever needs it. Nothing does: M5 x 16 already engages 9.7, which is the 2 x D aluminium asks for. |
| **NUT_TAP_DEPTH** | 12 mm | derived | NUT_TAP_REACH - 2 | 12, the working thread depth - NUT_TAP_REACH held back 2 mm so nothing can bottom. FLAG: IT IS MARGIN, NOT A STRENGTH REQUIREMENT, and an earlier version of this note overstated it as 'about half what aluminium asks'. His challenge, 2026-10-08: the load on these four bolts is SHEAR - the screw drives vertically and the bolts run horizontally - so why would thread depth matter? It matters only through preload: a bolted joint carries shear by FRICTION between the faces, and thread is what lets you develop the clamp load that makes the friction. Run the numbers and the joint was never short: at the as-supplied 8 mm thread an M5 reached 5.7, whose aluminium shear area strips at about 11 kN against the bolt's own ~9 kN proof - THE THREAD WAS ALREADY STRONGER THAN THE BOLT, which is what the 2 x D rule of thumb exists to achieve. So the deeper tap buys preload RETENTION, not capacity: aluminium relaxes, and more turns share the load. It costs five minutes in a soft material, which is the only reason it is worth doing at all. OPEN: THE BEARING BLOCKS CANNOT HAVE THIS - their hole is 8.7 against 6 of thread, so nothing to tap into; they are steel and do not need it. |

The sole bracket bolts UP into the inverted nut and there is nothing between them - no spacer, no shim - so this is the simplest of the nut joints: bolt less bracket. OPEN: SAME POINT AS THE Z: the load here is SHEAR and a bolted joint carries shear by friction, so what this joint needs is preload. The four holes are M5 clearance, so a joint that slips gives up lost motion the controller cannot see. Torque them properly and evenly. At the as-supplied 8 mm thread an M5 x 12 would reach 5.65 and the aluminium would still be stronger than the bolt - the deeper tap is margin. |
| **Z_NUT_BOLT_ENGAGE** | 9.7 mm | derived | BOLT_Z_NUT - Z_NUT_CBORE_WEB - NUT_SHIM | 9.7 mm into the nut housing, 1.94 x D in aluminium. It was 5.7 before the housing was tapped deeper, and FLAG: 5.7 WAS ALREADY ENOUGH - the aluminium thread strips at about 11 kN there against the bolt's ~9 kN proof load. The extra is margin against preload relaxation, not capacity. OPEN: WHAT THIS JOINT ACTUALLY NEEDS IS PRELOAD, NOT THREAD. The four bolts are in 6 mm clearance holes on M5, so 0.5 radial float per side - if the joint ever slips, that float becomes up to 1 mm of Z lost motion the controller cannot see. Friction is doing the work: at a modest 2 N.m each the four develop roughly 1.6 kN of friction capacity against a 500 N envelope. TORQUE THEM PROPERLY AND EVENLY; that matters more here than the last few millimetres of thread. Bounded at both ends like Z_BOLT_ENGAGE - too little and the thread strips, more than NUT_TAP_DEPTH and the bolt jams where the thread stops. |

FLAG: THE METHOD IS THE PART WORTH KEEPING, because it is not obvious and a future session would otherwise re-derive it badly: put ONE bearing block at each end of the same rail, each pushed until its grease zerk touches the end plate, and measure the INSIDE distance between them. That gap is (rail span) less TWO block bodies - and the real carriage IS two butted blocks, BLOCK_BUTTED, so the gap you measure is exactly the real carriage’s travel rather than a proxy for it. The zerks are necessarily on the blocks’ OUTER ends, since otherwise a pair could not butt, so the test reproduces the real stop geometry at both ends. The AS5311 datasheet gives usable stroke as the active area LESS the 2.0 mm Hall array, with the short poles at either edge of the strip excluded from the active area - so tape equal to travel is always short. And the carriage reaches its hard stops exactly when something has gone wrong, which is the worst moment for the reader to be off the end: a magnetic reader that leaves the tape and returns gives a wrong count and does not complain. At 30 a side the array never approaches an end pole, which retires the end-exclusion question rather than requiring it to be respected. |

The side plates go the other way and are fine: one washer, 40 less 29.529 is 10.471, inside the 11, and engagement caps at ACORN_NUT_THREAD's 10 rather than the old 9.571. SETTLED: THE REAR PLATE TAKES A THIRD WASHER AND KEEPS ITS M8 x 45 - his call 2026-10-12, so the stack lifts the nut 3.3, it protrudes 10.35 inside the 11, and it engages the full 10 of acorn thread. See the rear-plate-to-tongue joint in fasteners.toml. |

OPEN: AND THE TRADE RUNS BACKWARDS: thicker ribs DISPLACE SAND, and sand is about 1.5 g/cc against plywood's 0.68, so swapping rib volume for sand volume REDUCES total mass - paying plywood to remove ballast, on a box where mass is wanted for damping. SETTLED: THE SURPLUS 24 GOES TO THE BACK EDGE instead, which torsion-box.md names as the thing that deserves material: a beam supported at its midpoint carrying both back corners, which cannot be propped. SETTLED: THE LAMINATION RUNS ACROSS THE MACHINE BECAUSE OF THE CROSS TENON - the base's fore-aft rails pass THROUGH the leg as a through tenon formed by omitting the middle two strips at glue-up, so the mortise is 36 wide in X and runs the full POST_W_Y in Y. FLAG: 18 + 36 + 18 = 72 EXACTLY, so the rail is two laminations thick and the gap is two strips wide - the arithmetic is why the leg is four strips and not five. His, 2026-10-11, replacing screws into plywood. NOTE: THE PART IS A T-NUT - a pronged tee nut, three or four prongs. NOT a threaded insert, which has an external wood-screw thread and drives with a hex key, and NOT a hopper-feed T-nut, which is the flanged barrel with screw holes instead of prongs. The name is recorded because he asked for it and because the three get ordered interchangeably. SETTLED: THE ORIENTATION IS RIGHT AND IT IS THE THING USUALLY GOT WRONG: a T-nut goes on the face the bolt pulls TOWARD, so the flange bears on the wood and the prongs only stop it rotating. Bolt down from above, flange under the top skin. FLAG: THEY MUST GO IN BEFORE THE TOP SKIN IS GLUED TO THE RIBS. They are fitted from below and there is no access afterwards - the same hard ordering as assembly.md's rule about driving a screw into each post tenon before the skin goes on, and the same consequence for getting it wrong: a hole in the box. SETTLED: IT ANSWERS A REAL OBJECTION: with the angle in FRONT of the fin these fixings work in WITHDRAWAL if the fin tips backward, the opposite sense to the old behind-the-fin brackets, and a prong insert in the 25 top skin is a far better anchor than a screw. |
| **T_BOX_FRONT_CAP** | 24 mm | alias | T_BOX_TONGUE | 25 - the board capping the box's FRONT edge, same stock and thickness as the tongue on the other three sides, so every wall is the same 44 section with T_BOX_WALL_WEB. SETTLED: HIS, 2026-10-11, AND THE REASON IS THE POST: the front posts are ledged T_BOX_LEDGE deep like the others, leaving a 44 shoulder that expects a 44 wall - without this cap the front 25 of that shoulder would bear nothing. FLAG: IT IS NOT A TONGUE: it finishes flush with the top skin and stands NOTHING proud, so the apron stays a clear work surface. See BOX_FRONT_CAP_H. |
| **BOX_FRONT_CAP_H** | 142 mm | alias | BOX_THK | 144 - the front cap's height: the box's full thickness, capping the end grain of both skins exactly as the tongues do, finishing FLUSH with the top skin. SETTLED: ZERO PROUD, his words 2026-10-11 - so it will not project out. That is the ONE way the front differs from the other three sides, which stand BOX_TONGUE_PROUD above the skin. Compare TONGUE_FULL_H at 204 against this 144: the 60 between them is exactly the proud the front does not have. |
| **FIN_ANGLE_TO_RIB** | 46.35 mm | derived | SIDE_TONGUE_END + T_FIN - RIB_LAST_FRONT | 44.55 - from the LAST across-rib's front face to where the angle's horizontal leg begins. See FIN_BASE_TO_RIB, which is the figure that CLOSED the blocking question on 2026-10-11. |
| **FIN_ANGLE_T** | 6 mm | measured |  | 6 - the angle extrusion's wall thickness, his 2026-10-11. FLAG: IT WAS A NOMINAL 5 THAT I INVENTED, and the note then claimed it FED NOTHING - which was true when written and wrong within the hour: it sets how much bolt is used up before the thread, so it sizes FIN_ANGLE_BOLT_L. A symbol recorded as inert is exactly the one that quietly becomes load-bearing. The one place it could ever matter is the inside corner radius holding the vertical leg off the fin's face or the horizontal leg off the skin, which is a fit to check with the part in hand rather than a number to design to. |
| **BOX_SIDE_CAP_START** | 1006.35 mm | alias | SIDE_TONGUE_END | 1006.35 - where each SIDE CAP begins, which is exactly where the side tongue ends. SETTLED: HIS, 2026-10-11: the 25 front cap turns the corner and runs back down each side until it meets the side tongue, so the box's outer face is continuous all the way round. FLAG: IT CLOSES A GAP NOBODY HAD NAMED: the side tongue stops at SIDE_TONGUE_END and the box then runs on to BOX_FORE_AFT, so the side was BARE for that last stretch - and that is precisely where the front fin overhangs outboard by FIN_PROUD. His words: so the fin overhang will not look like it is hanging in midair. SETTLED: AND IT IS NOT ONLY LOOKS - the fin's outboard overhang now lands on the cap's top edge instead of on nothing. |
| **BOX_SIDE_CAP_L** | 204.65 mm | derived | BOX_FORE_AFT - SIDE_TONGUE_END | 203.65 - each side cap's run, from the side tongue's front end forward to the BOX'S FRONT EDGE, where the front cap laps across its end. FLAG: THE FRONT CAP IS THE CONTINUOUS ONE AND THE SIDE CAPS DIE INTO IT, which is the convention the back already uses - torsion-box.md: the front and back tongues run the full width and cover the end grain of the side tongue in a butt joint, so the side tongues die into them, not the other way round. OPEN: THIS SYMBOL READ 228.65 FOR ONE COMMIT, off BOX_FORE_AFT + T_BOX_FRONT_CAP, which is the OTHER build - side caps running out to the front cap's outer face with the front cap butting between them. Same outer shape, opposite lap, and the 3D model drew the first while the registry said the second. Caught by reading the generated figure against the drawn part rather than by any check. Same 25 stock, same BOX_FRONT_CAP_H height, flush with the top skin and nothing proud. NOTE: IT DERIVES FROM BOX_FORE_AFT, so it grows and shrinks with the apron - which is now a remainder, so it will. |
| **SIDE_LAM_L** | 1204.65 mm | derived | SIDE_TONGUE_L + BOX_SIDE_CAP_L | 1203.65 - each side's outer lamination CUT AS ONE PIECE, running the box's full depth from SIDE_TONGUE_START to the front edge, where the back and front laminations lap its end grain. FLAG: IT WAS BRIEFLY 1235 ON 2026-10-11, when he had the SIDE lap the BACK - his preference - and it was reverted the same day for money: at 1235 the side no longer fits beside the top skin on a 4 x 8 sheet, which costs a whole sheet of 25 mm at $245. OPEN: THE REVERSAL ALSO CAUSED A CLASH that reverting removes: running the side back to the box's back face put it through the rear plate's right end, which overhangs the box by 2.66 - and SIDE_TONGUE_START's 6.35 exists precisely to clear that plate. SETTLED: HIS BUILD CALL 2026-10-11: cut it full depth and TONGUE_FULL_H tall, then saw away the proud portion forward of SIDE_TONGUE_END where it is not wanted. FLAG: SO THE SIDE TONGUE AND THE SIDE CAP ARE ONE PART, NOT TWO - they were drawn and reasoned about as separate pieces, and this removes the butt joint at 1006.35 on each side. The step from 60 proud to flush becomes a SAW CUT rather than a joint. SETTLED: IT IS THE BETTER PART BREAKDOWN: a continuous lamination along the Y beam's whole bearing line, one part per side instead of two, and no end grain at the one place the beam is carried. OPEN: THE STOCK IS BIGGER: each side now wants a piece 1203.65 x 204 rather than two smaller ones, so it must be nested before the sheet is cut. The back and front still lap it - the back tongue caps its back end and the front cap laps its front end, which is the convention torsion-box.md already sets. |
| **SIDE_LAM_PROUD_CUT** | 1006.35 mm | alias | SIDE_TONGUE_END | 1006.35 - where the saw cut falls on each side lamination: BEHIND it the piece stands BOX_TONGUE_PROUD above the top skin as the tongue, AHEAD of it the top 60 is cut away so the piece finishes flush. SETTLED: IT IS SIDE_TONGUE_END BY CONSTRUCTION - the tongue is wanted exactly where the Y beam's outboard plate is bolted to it and nowhere else, and SIDE_TONGUE_END is already where the fin caps the beam. NOTE: THE CUT IS THE ONLY THING THAT CHANGES ALONG THE PIECE: thickness, height below the skin and the bolt line all run through unbroken. |

SETTLED: THE EXTRUSION COMES WITHOUT HOLES, so this is a pattern to drill rather than one to measure - which is why it is a stated part figure now. FLAG: IT WAS A NOMINAL 42.5 FOR FOUR BOLTS, invented when the piece was assumed to be pre-drilled and the note said so. Both the count and the basis were wrong: he drills his own, and three over 170 is enough. SETTLED: THE 85 LANDS ON THE MIDDLE of the 170 and the end margins match at 30 - see FIN_ANGLE_BOLT_END_MARGIN. |

FLAG: THE 15 OF EMPTY HOLE IS THE PART THAT SURPRISES. The T-nut is driven in from UNDERNEATH, so its thread occupies the BOTTOM 10 of a 25 skin and the top 15 is a clearance hole. Reading the skin as 'the bolt goes through 25 of wood into a nut' gets the length wrong by 15 - which is how an M8 x 25 was first specified. |
| **FIN_ANGLE_TNUT_THREAD** | 10 mm | part |  | 10 - the thread the pronged T-nuts he has actually provide. His, 2026-10-11. OPEN: IT IS THE BARREL'S THREAD AND NOT THE SKIN'S THICKNESS: the barrel sits in the lower 10 of the 25 skin, see FIN_ANGLE_BOLT_DEAD. |
| **FIN_ANGLE_BOLT_L** | 30 mm | part |  | M8 x 30, the small flange type - FLANGE_LOW_D and FLANGE_LOW_H. SETTLED: IT ENGAGES 9 OF THE 10: 30 less FIN_ANGLE_BOLT_DEAD's 21. FLAG: AN M8 x 25 WAS SPECIFIED FIRST AND WOULD HAVE ENGAGED 4 - under half a diameter - because the 15 of unthreaded hole above the T-nut was not counted. He caught it himself on being shown the stack. SETTLED: NOTHING BOTTOMS OUT: a T-nut is through-threaded, so a longer bolt would simply protrude into the cavity, which ends up full of sand. 35 would give the full 10 and protrude 4; 30 is enough and sits flush. |
| **FIN_T_BOLT_L** | 16 mm | part |  | M8 x 16 for T1 and T2 - the two through the angle's vertical leg into the fin's TAPPED holes. SETTLED: IT EQUALS FIN_ANGLE_T + FIN_BOLT_TAP_DEPTH EXACTLY, 6 + 10, so the thread uses the whole tapped depth and the bolt finishes FLUSH with the fin's back face. SETTLED: NOTHING PROTRUDES, which matters more here than it usually would: the tee track bed is hard against that face and is the whole reason the fin is tapped rather than through-bolted. NOTE: HE CHECKED THE SUPPLY AND 16 IS WHAT IS SOLD - a 15 was recorded for one commit off his first reading, and it would have engaged 9 and cost nothing either; the stocked size happens to be the exact one. A bolt here CANNOT BOTTOM OUT, the 10 fin being tapped THROUGH. |
| **FIN_ANGLE_BOLT_FIRST** | 30 mm | part |  | 30 - the first skin bolt from the angle's near end, which is the end that starts flush with the box's side edge. His, 2026-10-11. The three run 30, 85, 140 at FIN_ANGLE_BOLT_PITCH. |

FLAG: THE EXPRESSION CARRIES THE END BAY SEPARATELY since 2026-10-14, because the five bays are no longer equal: web, end bay, then three rib-and-bay steps, then the last rib's own thickness. Reading it as four equal pitches off the web gives 971.6 and is wrong by 0.6. Named because three separate questions measure from it, and because walking the rib pitch inline each time is how the three would drift apart. It follows the bay count and bay size, so it moves when the grid does. |

SETTLED: THIS IS THE NUMBER THAT CLOSED THE BLOCKING QUESTION, 2026-10-11, and it closed it as NOT NEEDED. lateral-stiffness.md had carried a general warning that bottom-edge bearing is only worth having if it lands on structure rather than on skin spanning between grid members - written before any rib layout existed to check it against. At 34.55 from a rib, a 25 top skin is not spanning anything; it is a short overhang off a support that is right there. His call, and the measurement is his too - he put the nearest rib at about 40 by eye. FLAG: IF THE FIN'S BEARING IS EVER WANTED HARDER, MOVE A RIB UNDER IT RATHER THAN ADDING BLOCKING - a rib is continuous and a block is not, and the grid is egg crate precisely because continuity is what gives two-way plate action. |

SETTLED: ALSO CLOSED AS NO BLOCKING, same day and same reasoning as FIN_BASE_TO_RIB, with one thing in its favour: these pull UP rather than bear down, and 25 of Baltic birch over a 67.55 reach against a hand-tightened M8 is nowhere near the weak link in that joint. NOTE: THE WEAK LINK IS THE T-NUT'S OWN GRIP ON THE PLYWOOD, which is why the prongs and the flange matter and the span does not. |

SETTLED: HIS REASONING, and it is stronger than he put it - he said the plate rests on the skin over the back of the box, which is true, and the figure says the footprint is wholly inside the wall rather than merely over it. |

SETTLED: IT IS A GRIP TERM, NOT A DETAIL: a counterbore REMOVES material the bolt would otherwise pass through, so it makes the grip SHORTER and the bolt reach FURTHER past the far face. The shelf bar's verticals are the only counterbored joint on the machine. |
| **SHELF_VERT_GRIP** | 42.8 mm | derived | SHELF_BAR_H - M8_SOCKET_CBORE | 42.8 - what the shelf bar's VERTICAL bolts cross: the bar's HEIGHT less the counterbore. FLAG: IT IS SHELF_BAR_H AND NOT SHELF_BAR_W, and the fastener schedule had the width. The verticals are counterbored FROM BELOW and run up through the 50.8 height into the beam's underside slot; it is the HORIZONTAL pair that cross the 25.4 width. Reading the wrong one made an M8 x 50 look 26.6 too long when it is right. |
| **LIMIT_SENSOR_H** | 17.75 mm | measured |  | The SN04-N's body height - his caliper 2026-10-13. SQUARE BODY, NOT A BARREL: these are the block type, so the mount clamps the body rather than threading an M18 nut either side, and there is no barrel length to trade against a lock nut. It is the height that sets how far the sensor stands above whatever it is bolted to, which is what the stepper frame's window has to clear. |
| **LIMIT_SENSOR_W** | 18.35 mm | measured |  | The SN04-N's body width - his caliper 2026-10-13. |
| **LIMIT_SENSOR_D** | 35 mm | measured |  | The SN04-N's body depth, SENSING FACE TO WIRE EXIT - his caliper 2026-10-13. FLAG: IT INCLUDES NO CABLE BEND RADIUS. The cable leaves the back face, so the space the part really occupies fore-aft is this plus whatever the wire needs to turn, and that is the figure a pocket or a window has to clear rather than the 35. |
| **LIMIT_SENSOR_BRACKET_D** | 20 mm | measured |  | 20 - what the metal bracket adds to the sensor's own depth, his 2026-10-13. FLAG: IT IS ADDED DEPTH, NOT THE BRACKET'S OWN SIZE: the sensor overlaps it, so the pair occupy LIMIT_SENSOR_STACK_D rather than the two parts summed. |
| **LIMIT_SENSOR_ADJUST** | 15 mm | measured |  | 15 of fore-aft adjustment in the bracket's slots, his 2026-10-13. SETTLED: THIS IS WHAT MAKES THE TRIP POINT A SETTING RATHER THAN A DIMENSION - the M3 pair in the casting's top face are fixed at LIMIT_SENSOR_M3_PITCH, and the slot takes up where the target actually lands. Nothing on a drawing has to predict the trip point to better than this. |
| **LIMIT_SENSOR_M3_PITCH** | 8 mm | part |  | 8 - the centres of the two M3 tapped into the stepper frame's top face, matching the bracket's slots. His scheme 2026-10-13. The frame is ferrous, so these are tapped into cast iron rather than aluminium - see machine/assembly.md. |
| **LIMIT_SENSOR_STACK_D** | 55 mm | derived | LIMIT_SENSOR_D + LIMIT_SENSOR_BRACKET_D | 55 - sensor plus bracket, fore-aft. OPEN: IT STILL CARRIES NO CABLE BEND. LIMIT_SENSOR_D is measured to the WIRE EXIT, not to the back of a turned cable, so a pocket or a window sized on this is sized on the metal and not on the installation. |
| **LIMIT_SENSOR_BRACKET_H** | 10 mm | measured |  | 10 - what the bracket adds in HEIGHT, his 2026-10-13, AS FLOPPED FOR THE FIRST TEST: the sensor sits ON TOP of the bracket rather than beneath it. SETTLED: BOTH ORIENTATIONS MOUNT, his 2026-10-14 - right side up as photographed fouls nothing anywhere, and inverted, nestled down inside the stepper casting frame, works too provided the sensor is held LIMIT_SENSOR_BK12_SETBACK clear of the BK12. So the bench test decides on SENSING alone and not on fit. FLAG: THE FLOP ITSELF IS STILL NOT SETTLED - it was made to get the sensing face away from the ferrous stepper frame, and whether that was necessary is the bench test. If the sensor goes back under the bracket this figure still applies but the stack height does not. |
| **LIMIT_SENSOR_BK12_SETBACK** | 10 mm | pinned |  | 10 - the LEAST the sensor may stand back from the BACK side of the BK12 bearing, and it applies ONLY to the inverted mount: his, 2026-10-14. SETTLED: IT IS WHAT MAKES THE INVERTED OPTION REAL - turned upside down the sensor nestles down inside the stepper casting frame rather than standing LIMIT_SENSOR_STACK_H above it, and at 10 clear of the BK12 it still works. NOTE: RIGHT SIDE UP, AS PHOTOGRAPHED, HAS NO SUCH CONSTRAINT - it fouls nothing anywhere. So this is the price of the option that gives the window its height back, not a constraint on the design as drawn. |
| **LIMIT_SENSOR_STACK_H** | 27.75 mm | derived | LIMIT_SENSOR_BRACKET_H + LIMIT_SENSOR_H | 27.75 - how far the sensor's top stands above the surface the bracket bolts to, flopped. THIS IS THE FIGURE THE WINDOW HAS TO CLEAR if the sensor sits over the part of the casting that passes through the plate. |
| **WINDOW_CORNER_R** | 10 mm | pinned |  | 10 - the corner radius on each rear plate window. FLAG: THE BINDING FEATURE IS A BOLT HEAD, NOT THE CASTING. The M5 x 35 rails bolt's head sits nearest the bottom-outboard corner, and WINDOW_CORNER_MARGIN is what is left between them. OPEN: THE MARGIN SHRINKS AS THE RADIUS GROWS - 1.2 at this 10, about 2.6 at a 6 - so a smaller radius is the safer direction, not the tighter one. The geometric limit is about 13, where the head touches the fillet. |
| **CAST_HEAD_X_IN** | 2.76 mm | derived | BF12_COL_INB - (M5_HEAD_D / 2) | 2.76 - how far in from the window's OUTBOARD edge the M5 x 35 rails bolt's head starts. The column is 7 off the beam's outer face and the window's outboard edge is that same face, so the head's own radius is all that separates them. |
| **CAST_HEAD_Z_UP** | 5 mm | derived | Y_BEAM_UNDERSIDE - T_INTERPOSER - CASTING_RAIL_H - M5_HEAD_H - WINDOW_Z_LOW | 5 - how far the same head's underside sits above the window's BOTTOM edge. Beam underside, less the bar, less the casting's rail depth, less the head itself. |
| **WINDOW_CORNER_MARGIN** | 1.2013 mm | derived | WINDOW_CORNER_R - (((WINDOW_CORNER_R - CAST_HEAD_X_IN) ** 2 + (WINDOW_CORNER_R - CAST_HEAD_Z_UP) ** 2) ** 0.5) | 1.2 - metal between the M5 x 35 head and the corner fillet, as the distance from the fillet's centre to the head's nearest point taken off the radius. FLAG: IT MUST NOT GO NEGATIVE. Negative means the fillet has eaten into the head's footprint and the bolt cannot be driven. Nothing bears here, so 1.2 is a clearance rather than a stress question - but it is the figure that moves if the radius, the bolt column or the head size changes, and it is checked rather than remembered. |
| **SOLE_TIP_W** | 46 mm | pinned |  | 46 - the sole bracket's width at its TIP. FLAG: IT IS A FREE FIGURE AND SHEET 5 SAYS SO - nothing mates to the narrow end, so unlike the 98.19 reach it is chosen rather than derived. That is what makes a T-shaped bracket a question of preference rather than of fit: the root must stay XEP_W wide for DOUBLER_SEATING, because that is where the eight root bolts land on the end plate and doubler end faces, and everything past it is metal removal. |
| **SOLE_BASE_D** | 24.38 mm | alias | DOUBLER_SEATING | 24.38 - the T's base depth, outboard from the end plate's face. IT IS NOT A CHOICE: it is the X end plate's end face plus the doubler's behind it, which is the full seating the eight root bolts land on. His read off the model, 2026-10-13 - 'it's showing 24, that's all you need'. |
| **SOLE_STEM_W** | 46 mm | alias | SOLE_TIP_W | 46 - the T's stem width, carried straight out from the base rather than tapering. It is SOLE_TIP_W because the tip is what has to take the nut's four bolts and nothing else constrains it; the trapezoid arrived at the same 46 at the same place. |
| **SOLE_STEM_L** | 73.81 mm | alias | SOLE_REACH | 73.81 - how far the stem runs past the base to reach the nut. SOLE_BASE_D + SOLE_STEM_L closes on SOLE_BRACKET_L, which is the check that the T covers the same reach the trapezoid did. |
| **SOLE_FILLET_R** | 6 mm | pinned |  | 6 - the radius where the stem meets the base, both sides. His, 2026-10-13, for looks rather than for stress, and a plasma or waterjet path walks it for nothing. FLAG: THE 3D MODEL DRAWS THIS CORNER SQUARE. Its prism profile is a polygon and a fillet would be an approximation that then disagrees with the sheet; the radius lives here and on the drawing instead. |
| **SOLE_T_CHECK** | 0 mm | derived | SOLE_BRACKET_L - (SOLE_BASE_D + SOLE_STEM_L) | 0 - and it must stay 0. The T's base plus its stem has to reach exactly as far as the trapezoid did, because the reach is set by the nut and not by the outline. |
